characters.name: Antoine
characters.personality: brisk, friendly, proud of the house specialities

characters.name: Martine
characters.personality: warm, chatty, a bit curious; the neighbour from chapter 1

characters.name: Camille
characters.personality: warm, cheerful, always in a rush; the acquaintance from chapter 1, now a friend

notes: Vous with the waiter, the shop assistant, the ticket clerk, the passer-by and the neighbour Martine, as in chapter 1; tu only with Camille, presented as the chapter 1 acquaintance who has become a friend. Please confirm the switch to tu feels natural.
The learner's lines default to the masculine as in chapter 1 (désolé, fils unique, mon ami); feminine forms are given in the notes and need their own recording where the sound differs (fille unique).
Wordings to check first: « Alors, ça vous a plu ? » from a bouchon waiter, « Vous l’avez en plus grand ? », « Je dois descendre à quelle gare ? », « J’appelle le 15 ? ».
Facts to verify: 96 euros for two returns Lyon–Marseille, the 14:10 departure from platform C at Part-Dieu, emergency numbers 15 and 112.

scene.en: A lively bouchon, one of Lyon's small traditional restaurants, on a busy evening; the waiter is proud of the homemade quenelles.

lines.text: Bonsoir ! Vous êtes combien ?
lines.pron: Link vous and êtes: voo-ZET. Combien: kon-BYAN, both vowels nasal.

en.m: Good evening! How many are you?
en.n: Bonsoir replaces bonjour from about 6 p.m. A bouchon is one of Lyon's small traditional restaurants; they fill up fast, so book ahead when you can.
en.l: good-evening! you are how-many

lines.text: Une table pour deux, s’il vous plaît.
lines.pron: Deux: say 'duh' with rounded lips; the x is silent.

en.n: Change the number: pour une personne, pour trois, pour quatre. Wait to be shown to a table rather than seating yourself.
en.l: a table for two, if it you pleases

lines.text: Qu’est-ce que vous nous conseillez ?
lines.pron: Qu’est-ce que is just two beats: KESS-kuh. Conseillez: kon-say-YAY.

en.n: Conseiller (to advise) is the usual verb for this. Qu’est-ce que is the everyday way to start a 'what' question. Eating alone, say me instead of nous.
en.l: what is-it that you to-us advise

lines.text: La quenelle de brochet, elle est faite maison.
lines.pron: Quenelle: kuh-NELL. Brochet: bro-SHAY, with a silent t.

en.n: A quenelle is a light, oven-baked pike dumpling, Lyon's signature dish. Naming the thing first, then picking it up with elle, is typical of spoken French. Fait maison = homemade.
en.l: the quenelle of pike, she is made house

lines.text: Qu’est-ce qu’il y a dedans ?
lines.pron: Run it together: kess-keel-YAH duh-DAHN.

en.n: Il y a = there is, there are; dedans = inside. For an allergy, ask: Il y a des fruits à coque dedans ? (nuts), du lait ? (milk), du gluten ?
en.l: what is-it that it there has inside

lines.text: Du brochet, avec une sauce aux écrevisses.
lines.pron: Écrevisses: ay-kruh-VEESS.

en.n: Du (de + le) means 'some': du brochet, du pain, du fromage. Aux (à + les) names a flavour or main ingredient: sauce aux écrevisses, tarte aux pommes.
en.l: some pike, with a sauce to-the crayfish

lines.text: Je vais prendre la quenelle, s’il vous plaît.
lines.pron: Prendre: PRAHN-druh, with a nasal 'an'.

en.n: Je vais prendre (I'm going to take) is the natural way to order. Swap in any dish: je vais prendre le plat du jour, the dish of the day.
en.l: I go to-take the quenelle, if it you pleases

lines.text: Alors, ça vous a plu ?
lines.pron: Plu has the French u: say 'ee' with tightly rounded lips.

en.n: Plaire works the other way round from 'to like': ça vous a plu = that pleased you. Waiters ask this as they clear the plates; you will also hear the shorter Ça a été ?
en.l: so, that to-you has pleased

lines.text: Oui, c’était délicieux !
lines.pron: Délicieux: day-lee-SYUH; the x is silent.

en.n: C’était (it was) for a meal you have just finished; c’est délicieux while you are still eating. A simpler option: c’était très bon.

lines.text: On peut avoir l’addition, s’il vous plaît ?
lines.pron: Peut rhymes with deux: 'puh' with rounded lips, silent t.

en.m: Can we have the bill, please?
en.n: On is everyday French for 'we'; its verb stays singular: on peut. The bill only comes when you ask for it. Service is included, so a tip is just a few coins if you were happy.
en.l: one can have the addition, if it you pleases

lines.text: Vous avez une table pour deux ?
lines.pron: Link vous and avez: voo-zah-VAY.

en.m: Do you have a table for two?
en.n: A statement said with a rising voice is the normal spoken question. Handy when you walk in without a reservation (sans réservation).
en.l: you have a table for two

lines.text: Pour moi, le plat du jour, s’il vous plaît.
lines.pron: Plat: plah, with a silent t. Jour: zhoor.

en.m: For me, the dish of the day, please.
en.n: Pour moi + the dish: the easiest way to order, no verb needed. The plat du jour is the daily special, usually the best value at lunchtime.
en.l: for me, the dish of-the day, if it you pleases

scene.en: A small clothes shop on the Presqu’île, Lyon's central shopping district; the assistant is attentive and the sizes run small.

lines.text: Bonjour ! Je peux vous aider ?
lines.pron: Link vous and aider: voo-zeh-DAY.

en.n: Always say bonjour when you walk into a French shop: skipping it comes across as rude.
en.l: good-day! I can you help

lines.text: Merci, je regarde seulement.
lines.pron: Seulement: suhl-MAHN, ending on a nasal vowel with no n or t sound.

en.n: French has no separate '-ing' form: je regarde means both 'I look' and 'I'm looking'.
en.l: thanks, I look only

lines.text: En fait, je cherche un pull.
lines.pron: Pull has the French u (lips rounded, tongue forward): it does not sound like English 'pull'. The t of fait is usually silent.

en.m: Actually, I'm looking for a sweater.
en.n: Chercher already means 'to look for': never add pour. Un pull is short for pull-over. False friend: actuellement means 'currently'; 'actually' is en fait.
en.l: in fact, I seek a sweater

lines.text: Bien sûr. Celui-ci est en taille S.
lines.pron: Taille rhymes with English 'tie': tah-y.

en.m: Of course. This one is a size S.
en.n: Celui-ci = this one, for a masculine noun (celle-ci for a feminine one). French sizes often run small. Size letters are said the French way: S is 'ess', M is 'em', L is 'el'.
en.l: well sure. this-one-here is in size S

lines.text: Vous l’avez en plus grand ?
lines.pron: Plus here is 'plü' with a silent s; grand ends in a nasal vowel with a silent d: grahn.

en.m: Do you have it in a bigger size?
en.n: Plus grand = bigger; plus petit = smaller. L’ stands for le pull and goes before the verb: vous l’avez.
en.l: you it have in more big

lines.text: Oui, voilà un M.

en.n: Voilà is what you hear whenever someone hands you something. To try it on, ask: Je peux l’essayer ? The fitting rooms are les cabines.
en.l: yes, there-is an M

lines.text: Il coûte combien ?
lines.pron: Coûte: koot. The circumflex on û does not change the sound.

en.n: Il because pull is masculine; say elle coûte combien ? for a feminine item such as une veste (a jacket). The question word often comes last in spoken French.
en.l: it costs how-much

lines.text: Quarante-neuf euros.
lines.pron: kah-rahnt-NUHF uh-ROH: the f of neuf is pronounced, the s of euros is silent.

en.n: The price on the tag is the price you pay: tax is always included in France.

lines.text: Parfait, je le prends.
lines.pron: Prends: nasal 'an', silent d and s: prahn.

en.n: Le for a masculine item, la for a feminine one: je la prends. French uses the present tense where English says 'I'll take'.
en.l: perfect, I it take

lines.text: Vous prenez la carte ?
lines.pron: Prenez: pruh-NAY.

en.n: La carte is short for la carte bancaire (bank card). Cash is en espèces, or du liquide. Small shops sometimes set a minimum for card payments.
en.l: you take the card

lines.text: Vous l’avez dans une autre couleur ?
lines.pron: Couleur: koo-LUHR.

en.m: Do you have it in another colour?
en.n: Couleur is feminine: une autre couleur. Colours go after the noun: un pull bleu, un pull noir, un pull rouge.
en.l: you it have in an other colour

scene.en: The ticket office at Lyon Part-Dieu station on a busy afternoon; you and a friend want the next TGV to Marseille.

lines.text: Bonjour, je voudrais un billet pour Marseille.
lines.pron: Billet: bee-YAY (ll sounds like y, the t is silent). Marseille: mar-SAY, ending in a light y.

en.m: Hello, I'd like a ticket to Marseille.
en.n: Pour gives the destination on a ticket: un billet pour Paris. Un billet is for trains and planes; un ticket is for the metro, bus or tram.
en.l: good-day, I would-like a ticket for Marseille

lines.text: Un aller simple ou un aller-retour ?
lines.pron: Aller-retour: ah-lay ruh-TOOR.

en.n: Aller = the trip out, retour = the trip back. You will see the same two words on the ticket machines.
en.l: a going simple or a going-return

lines.text: Un aller-retour, s’il vous plaît.

en.n: For a one-way trip, say: un aller simple, s’il vous plaît.
en.l: a going-return, if it you pleases

lines.text: À quelle heure part le prochain train ?
lines.pron: The h of heure is silent, so quelle links to it: keh-LUHR. Train ends on the nasal vowel of vin, with no n sound.

en.m: What time does the next train leave?
en.n: Partir = to leave; arriver = to arrive. After à quelle heure the verb comes before its subject: part le train.
en.l: at what hour leaves the next train

lines.text: Il part à quatorze heures dix, voie C.
lines.pron: Link quatorze and heures: kah-tor-ZUHR. Dix is 'deess' at the end of a phrase.

en.m: It leaves at 14:10, from platform C.
en.n: Timetables use the 24-hour clock: quatorze heures = 2 p.m. The minutes simply follow heures. Voie = platform (literally 'track'); at Part-Dieu the platforms have letters.
en.l: it leaves at fourteen hours ten, track C

lines.text: Deux billets, s’il vous plaît.
lines.pron: duh bee-YAY: the s of billets is silent.

en.n: The plural s is silent: billet and billets sound exactly the same. You hear the plural in the number or the article.

lines.text: Je dois descendre à quelle gare ?
lines.pron: Descendre: day-SAHN-druh (sc sounds like s). Dois: dwah.

en.m: Which station do I have to get off at?
en.n: Devoir + infinitive = to have to: je dois descendre. Une gare is a railway station; un arrêt is a bus or tram stop; une station is for the metro.
en.l: I must go-down at which station

lines.text: À Marseille Saint-Charles, c’est le terminus.
lines.pron: Saint-Charles: san-SHARL, with a silent final s. Terminus: tehr-mee-NÜSS, where the final s is pronounced.

en.m: At Marseille Saint-Charles, it's the last stop.
en.n: Saint-Charles is Marseille's main station. Le terminus is the end of the line: you cannot miss it.
en.l: at Marseille Saint-Charles, it is the terminus

lines.text: Je peux payer par carte ?
lines.pron: Payer: peh-YAY. Peux: 'puh' with rounded lips, silent x.

en.n: Par carte = by card; en espèces = in cash. Je peux + infinitive is the easy way to ask whether you may do something.
en.l: I can pay by card

lines.text: Bien sûr. Ça fait quatre-vingt-seize euros.
lines.pron: kat-ruh-van-SEZ: vingt is a nasal 'van' with silent g and t.

en.m: Of course. That comes to ninety-six euros.
en.n: Ça fait (that makes) announces a total. French builds 80 as quatre-vingts, 'four twenties', so 96 is four-twenty-sixteen. Belgian and Swiss French say nonante-six.
en.l: well sure. that makes four-twenty-sixteen euros

lines.text: Un aller simple pour Marseille, s’il vous plaît.
lines.pron: Simple: SAM-pluh, starting with a nasal vowel.

en.n: No verb needed: naming what you want and adding s’il vous plaît is perfectly polite at a counter.
en.l: a going simple for Marseille, if it you pleases

scene.en: On Place Bellecour on a hot afternoon, the friend you are walking with suddenly feels faint; a passer-by stops to help.

lines.text: S’il vous plaît, j’ai besoin d’aide !
lines.pron: Besoin: buh-ZWAN, with a nasal ending. Aide sounds like 'ed'.

en.n: Avoir besoin de = to need (literally 'to have need of'). In an emergency in France, dial 15 for medical help (the SAMU) or 112, the European emergency number.
en.l: if it you pleases, I have need of help

lines.text: Qu’est-ce qui se passe ?
lines.pron: KESS-kee suh PASS.

en.n: Qu’est-ce qui (not que) because 'what' is the subject of the verb. Se passer = to happen.
en.l: what is-it that itself passes

lines.text: Mon ami ne se sent pas bien.
lines.pron: Link mon and ami: mo-nah-MEE. Sent: 'sahn', nasal, with a silent t.

en.n: For a woman, write mon amie: it sounds the same, and it is still mon (not ma) before a vowel. Ne and pas wrap around se sent to make it negative.
en.l: my friend not himself feels not well

lines.text: Il a très mal à la tête.
lines.pron: Tête: 'tet', with an open 'eh'.

en.n: Avoir mal à + body part = to have a pain there: mal au ventre (stomach), mal au dos (back). For a woman: elle a très mal à la tête.
en.l: he has very bad at the head

lines.text: Ne vous inquiétez pas. J’appelle le 15 ?
lines.pron: Inquiétez: an-kyay-TAY, starting with a nasal vowel. 15 is quinze: kanz.

en.n: The 15 (le quinze) is the SAMU, the emergency medical service. A present-tense statement said with a rising voice works as an offer: j’appelle ? = shall I call?
en.l: not yourself worry not. I call the 15

lines.text: Non merci. Il y a une pharmacie par ici ?
lines.pron: Pharmacie: far-mah-SEE. Il y a runs together: eel-YAH.

en.m: No thanks. Is there a pharmacy around here?
en.n: Il y a = there is; par ici = around here. French pharmacists give advice on minor problems; look for the flashing green cross.
en.l: no thanks. it there has a pharmacy by here

lines.text: Oui, il y en a une juste en face.
lines.pron: eel-yahn-NAH ün: the n of en links to a.

en.m: Yes, there's one just across the street.
en.n: En stands for 'of them': il y en a une = there is one (of them). En face = opposite, across the street.
en.l: yes, it there of-them has one just in face

lines.text: D’accord, j’ai compris. Merci pour votre aide !
lines.pron: Compris: kon-PREE, with a silent s.

en.m: OK, I've understood. Thank you for your help!
en.n: J’ai compris (I have understood) is the passé composé: avoir + past participle. Merci pour + noun: merci pour votre aide, merci pour tout.
en.l: of agreement, I have understood. thanks for your help

lines.text: Vous pouvez appeler un médecin ?
lines.pron: Médecin: mayd-SAN, two syllables, with a nasal ending.

en.n: A doctor is un médecin; docteur is mostly a title, as in Bonjour, docteur. False friend: la médecine is the science; a medicine you take is un médicament.
en.l: you can to-call a doctor

lines.text: Au secours !
lines.pron: oh suh-KOOR.

en.n: What you shout in real danger. À l’aide ! means the same.
en.l: to-the rescue

scene.en: Your neighbour Martine has invited you to Sunday lunch with her family; she keeps filling your plate and wants to know all about your own family.

lines.text: Entrez, entrez ! Faites comme chez vous.
lines.pron: Entrez: ahn-TRAY. Chez: shay.

en.m: Come in, come in! Make yourself at home.
en.n: Martine still says vous to you, and you to her: normal between neighbours until one of you suggests tu. Bring a small gift: flowers, chocolates or a bottle of wine.
en.l: enter, enter! do as at-the-home-of you

lines.text: Votre gratin est vraiment très bon !
lines.pron: Gratin: grah-TAN, with a nasal ending. Bon is one nasal vowel: no n sound.

en.m: Your gratin is really very good!
en.n: Bon (good) for food; bien is for how something is done. Gratin dauphinois, sliced potatoes baked in cream, comes from the Dauphiné, the region next door to Lyon.

lines.text: Merci ! Et vous parlez très bien français !
lines.pron: Français: frahn-SEH; ç always sounds like s.

en.m: Thank you! And you speak French very well!
en.n: Bien (well) goes right after the verb, before the language: vous parlez bien français.
en.l: thanks! and you speak very well French

lines.text: Merci, mais j’ai encore beaucoup à apprendre.
lines.pron: Apprendre: ah-PRAHN-druh. Beaucoup: boh-KOO, with a silent p.

en.m: Thank you, but I still have a lot to learn.
en.n: In France a compliment is often answered with a little modesty rather than a plain thank-you. Encore = still; beaucoup à + infinitive = a lot to (do).
en.l: thanks, but I have still much to learn

lines.text: Vous avez des petits-enfants ?
lines.pron: Three links in a row: voo-zah-VAY day puh-tee-zahn-FAHN.

en.n: Petits-enfants (literally 'little children') = grandchildren; grandparents are grands-parents. Des cannot be dropped the way 'any' or 'some' can in English.
en.l: you have some little-children

lines.text: Oui, deux ! Et vous, vous avez des frères et sœurs ?
lines.pron: Sœur: like English 'sir' said with rounded lips. Frères: frehr, with a silent s.

en.m: Yes, two! And you, do you have brothers and sisters?
en.n: Et vous ? hands a question back. French has no everyday word for 'siblings': you say frères et sœurs.
en.l: yes, two! and you, you have some brothers and sisters

lines.text: J’ai un grand frère et une petite sœur.
lines.pron: Petite: the second t is pronounced (puh-TEET) because of the final e; in petit it is silent.

en.m: I have an older brother and a younger sister.
en.n: Grand and petit also mean older and younger for brothers and sisters. Adjectives agree with the noun: un petit frère, une petite sœur.
en.l: I have a big brother and a little sister

lines.text: Et vous restez longtemps à Lyon ?
lines.pron: Lyon: lee-ON, a nasal 'on' with no n sound. Longtemps: lon-TAHN.

en.m: And are you staying long in Lyon?
en.n: False friend: rester means 'to stay', not 'to rest' (se reposer). À + city: à Lyon, à Paris.
en.l: and you stay long-time at Lyon

lines.text: Je ne sais pas encore.
lines.pron: Sais: 'seh', with a silent s.

en.n: Pas encore = not yet. In fast speech the ne is often dropped and you will hear something like 'shay pah'; keep ne and pas when you speak carefully.
en.l: I not know not yet

lines.text: Je suis fils unique.
lines.pron: Fils: feess (the l is silent, the s is pronounced). Unique: ü-NEEK.

en.n: Fils unique (literally 'only son') for a man; a woman says fille unique. No article after je suis here.
en.l: I am son only

lines.text: C’est un régal !
lines.pron: Régal: ray-GAL.

en.n: A warm compliment on food that hosts love to hear. You can also say je me régale: I'm really enjoying this.

scene.en: Camille, whom you met in your first days, is now a friend, so you say tu to each other; she suggests the park on Saturday, but that day doesn't suit you.

lines.text: Ça te dit d’aller au parc de la Tête d’Or samedi ?
lines.pron: Tête d’Or: tet-DOR. Samedi: sam-DEE, two syllables.

en.m: Do you fancy going to the Tête d’Or park on Saturday?
en.n: Ça te dit ? (does that say something to you?) = do you feel like it? The Parc de la Tête d’Or is Lyon's big park, with a lake and a free zoo. No word for 'on' before a day: samedi = on Saturday.
en.l: that to-you says to go to-the park of the Head of-Gold Saturday

lines.text: Désolé, samedi je ne peux pas.
lines.pron: Peux: 'puh' with rounded lips; the x is silent.

en.n: A woman writes désolée; it sounds the same. With friends you say tu, but an apology like this one needs no 'you' at all.
en.l: sorry, Saturday I not can not

lines.text: Dimanche, ça te va ?
lines.pron: Dimanche: dee-MAHNSH, with a nasal 'an'.

en.n: Ça te va ? (does that go for you?) = does that suit you? To someone you say vous to: ça vous va ?
en.l: Sunday, that to-you goes

lines.text: Oui, dimanche, ça marche !

en.n: Ça marche (literally 'that walks') is the casual way to say 'that works' or 'OK, deal'.
en.l: yes, Sunday, that walks

lines.text: On fait un pique-nique ?
lines.pron: Pique-nique: peek-NEEK.

en.n: On + present tense, said with a rising voice, is how friends suggest something: on y va ? (shall we go?). French 'makes' a picnic: faire un pique-nique.
en.l: one makes a picnic

lines.text: On se retrouve à midi ?
lines.pron: Retrouve: ruh-TROOV.

en.n: Se retrouver = to meet up (literally 'to find each other again'). Midi is noon and minuit is midnight; neither takes heures.
en.l: one each-other finds-again at midday

lines.text: Super ! Et après, on va boire un verre ?
lines.pron: Verre sounds just like vert (green): vehr.

en.m: Great! And afterwards, shall we go for a drink?
en.n: Boire un verre (to drink a glass) = to go for a drink, whatever you order. Aller + infinitive: on va boire.
en.l: super! and after, one goes to-drink a glass

lines.text: Oui, avec plaisir !
lines.pron: Plaisir: pleh-ZEER; an s between two vowels sounds like z.

en.n: Avec plaisir (with pleasure) works with friends and strangers alike. More casual still: carrément ! (totally!).
en.l: yes, with pleasure

lines.text: Alors, à dimanche midi !
lines.pron: Alors: ah-LOR, with a silent s.

en.m: So, see you Sunday at noon!
en.n: À + a day or a time is how you say 'see you then': à dimanche, à demain (tomorrow), à ce soir (tonight).
en.l: so, to Sunday midday

lines.text: Et si on allait au cinéma ?
lines.pron: Allait: ah-LEH.

en.m: How about going to the cinema?
en.n: Et si on + imperfect (allait) = 'what if we…?': a soft way to suggest something. Au = à + le. Friends often shorten cinéma to ciné.
en.l: and if one was-going to-the cinema

lines.text: C’est gentil, mais samedi je travaille.
lines.pron: Travaille: trah-VAH-y. Gentil: zhahn-TEE, with a silent l.

en.m: That's kind, but I'm working on Saturday.
en.n: Saying c’est gentil first softens the refusal. Je travaille is the present tense, used here for a fixed plan in the near future.
en.l: it is kind, but Saturday I work
